title: How do you capture a heap dump in Kubernetes where containers are ephemeral and an OOMKill can wipe the evidence — enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` with `-XX:HeapDumpPath` pointing at a MOUNTED volume (not `/tmp`), raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` so a large dump can finish writing, and distinguish a Kubernetes `OOMKilled` (cgroup/container-limit exceeded) from a Java `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` (heap only)?
shortTitle: How do you capture a heap dump in Kubernetes?

s1_definition.profdef: In Kubernetes, containers are ephemeral, so a heap dump written to the container's local filesystem is lost when the pod restarts. To preserve it you enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and point `-XX:HeapDumpPath` at a mounted persistent volume, not an ephemeral path like `/tmp`, and you raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` so a large dump has time to finish writing before the container is killed. You must also distinguish two different failures: a Kubernetes `OOMKilled`, where the container exceeded its cgroup memory limit counting all native and Java memory and the Linux kernel killed the process, versus a Java `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`, where only the Java heap filled while total container memory may have been fine.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a temporary audit office that National Bank of India sets up inside a rented room; when the lease ends the room is cleared out completely. If the auditor writes his findings on the room's whiteboard, they vanish when the room is returned. So you tell him to write findings into a briefcase he carries out with him (a mounted volume), not the whiteboard (ephemeral `/tmp`), and you give him a few extra minutes before the landlord locks the door (grace period) so he can finish writing. You also learn to tell two situations apart: the landlord evicting the whole office because it used more total space than allowed (OOMKilled), versus the auditor's own filing cabinet overflowing while the office as a whole had room (Java heap OutOfMemoryError).
s1_definition.oneliner: In Kubernetes, write the heap dump to a mounted volume with a long enough grace period so an ephemeral pod does not wipe it, and distinguish OOMKilled, which is the container exceeding its total memory limit, from a Java heap OutOfMemoryError, which is only the heap filling.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Kubernetes, containers are ephemeral, so a heap dump written to the container's local filesystem is lost when the pod restarts. To preserve it you enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and point `-XX:HeapDumpPath` at a mounted persistent volume, not an ephemeral path like `/tmp`, and you raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` so a large dump has time to finish writing before the container is killed. You must also distinguish two different failures: a Kubernetes `OOMKilled`, where the container exceeded its cgroup memory limit counting all native and Java memory and the Linux kernel killed the process, versus a Java `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`, where only the Java heap filled while total container memory may have been fine.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a temporary audit office that National Bank of India sets up inside a rented room; when the lease ends the room is cleared out completely. If the auditor writes his findings on the room's whiteboard, they vanish when the room is returned. So you tell him to write findings into a briefcase he carries out with him (a mounted volume), not the whiteboard (ephemeral `/tmp`), and you give him a few extra minutes before the landlord locks the door (grace period) so he can finish writing. You also learn to tell two situations apart: the landlord evicting the whole office because it used more total space than allowed (OOMKilled), versus the auditor's own filing cabinet overflowing while the office as a whole had room (Java heap OutOfMemoryError).

**One line to remember:** In Kubernetes, write the heap dump to a mounted volume with a long enough grace period so an ephemeral pod does not wipe it, and distinguish OOMKilled, which is the container exceeding its total memory limit, from a Java heap OutOfMemoryError, which is only the heap filling.

sections.s2_technical:
The ephemeral-container problem is the heart of this. When a Java process throws an OutOfMemoryError you want a heap dump to analyze, and `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` tells the JVM to write one automatically at the moment of failure. The trap in Kubernetes is where it writes. By default or by habit people point `-XX:HeapDumpPath` at something like `/tmp`, but a container's filesystem is wiped when the pod restarts, and an OutOfMemoryError usually leads to a restart, so the dump you most need disappears with the evidence. The fix is to point `-XX:HeapDumpPath` at a path backed by a mounted volume, typically a PersistentVolumeClaim, so the dump file survives the pod's death and you can retrieve it afterward. For example, `-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps` where `/var/dumps` is a mounted PVC.

Writing a heap dump of a multi-gigabyte heap takes time, often many seconds. Kubernetes, when it decides to stop a pod, sends a termination signal and then waits only `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, thirty seconds by default, before forcibly killing it. If the dump is still being written when that window closes, you get a truncated, useless file. So you raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to a value large enough for the dump to finish, which gives the JVM time to flush the full dump to the mounted volume. You also size the volume to hold a dump roughly the size of the heap plus overhead.

Now the crucial diagnostic distinction. A Java `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` is thrown by the JVM itself when the Java heap, bounded by `-Xmx`, cannot satisfy an allocation; it is a Java-level exception, it triggers the heap-dump-on-OOM behavior, and total container memory may have been perfectly healthy. A Kubernetes `OOMKilled`, by contrast, is the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminating the process because the container exceeded its cgroup memory limit, and that limit counts everything the process uses: the Java heap plus Metaspace plus thread stacks plus the Code Cache plus direct and native memory plus the JVM's own overhead. An OOMKilled is not a Java exception at all; the process is killed abruptly, so often no heap dump is written because the JVM never got to run its handler.

You tell them apart by where you look. For OOMKilled, `kubectl describe pod` shows the container's last state with `Reason: OOMKilled` and a non-zero exit code, typically one hundred thirty-seven, and `kubectl top pod` shows memory at the limit. For a Java heap OutOfMemoryError, the application logs contain the `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` stack trace and the heap dump is produced. The senior-level insight is that these point to different fixes: a Java heap OOM means the heap is too small or there is a heap leak, fixed by raising `-Xmx` or fixing the leak, while an OOMKilled with a healthy heap means native memory, such as direct buffers, thread stacks, or Metaspace, is the culprit, and you investigate with Native Memory Tracking, `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary`, rather than a heap dump. A classic banking production incident is a service sized with a generous `-Xmx` that equals the container limit, leaving no room for Metaspace and thread stacks, so it gets OOMKilled while the heap graphs look fine, and the fix is to set `-Xmx` well below the container limit or use the container-aware `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` flag so the JVM reserves headroom for non-heap memory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's payments service running in Kubernetes kept getting OOMKilled at night, but the heap dumps were gone because they were written to `/tmp` and wiped on restart. This is exactly the ephemeral-container problem, solved by writing the dump to a mounted volume and raising the grace period.

Problem 2 — The team could not tell whether it was a Java heap problem or a native-memory problem, because the heap graphs looked healthy yet the container was killed. This is exactly the OOMKilled-versus-Java-heap-OutOfMemoryError distinction, where the container limit counts all memory, not just the heap.

In the mini-project we build a small demo that programmatically triggers a Java heap OutOfMemoryError into a configurable dump path, and a reporter that reads total heap versus non-heap usage to illustrate why container memory can be exhausted even when the heap is fine. We log the flags and kubectl checks used to distinguish the two failures.

##### 4b. Deployment (volume + grace period)

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml — preserve the dump and give it time to write
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120      # let a large dump finish writing
      containers:
        - name: payments
          image: bank/payments:1.0.0
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: "1Gi"                    # cgroup hard cap (ALL memory)
          env:
            - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
              # -Xmx BELOW the limit → headroom for Metaspace/stacks/direct
              value: >-
                -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60.0
                -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
                -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps
          volumeMounts:
            - name: heapdumps
              mountPath: /var/dumps            # MOUNTED, survives pod restart
      volumes:
        - name: heapdumps
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: heapdumps-pvc
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/k8sdump/K8sHeapDumpDemo.java

# Force a JAVA HEAP OOM locally to see the dump get written
java -Xms64m -Xmx64m \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=./payments.hprof \
     -cp out com.bank.k8sdump.K8sHeapDumpDemo --force-heap-oom

# In the cluster, distinguish the two failures:
kubectl describe pod payments-service-xxxx   # look for Reason: OOMKilled, exit 137
kubectl top pod payments-service-xxxx         # memory at the cgroup limit?
# If OOMKilled but heap healthy, inspect NATIVE memory:
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary           # needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a service configured with a one-gigabyte container limit, a heap capped below that, a mounted dump volume, and a one-hundred-twenty-second grace period.

Step 1: At startup the breakdown reporter logs heap and non-heap usage, showing that the container's memory budget covers both plus native memory, not just the heap.

Step 2: The demo logs the exact flags that preserve evidence: heap dump on OutOfMemoryError, a dump path on a mounted volume rather than ephemeral storage, a raised grace period, and a heap maximum set below the container limit to leave headroom.

Step 3: If run with the force flag, the demo allocates ten-megabyte chunks until the Java heap is exhausted and the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError Java heap space. Because heap-dump-on-OOM is enabled, the JVM writes a dump to the configured path, which in the cluster would be the mounted volume that survives the restart.

Step 4: The demo contrasts this with OOMKilled, explaining that an OOMKilled is not a Java exception; the kernel kills the process for exceeding the container's total memory limit, often before the JVM can write any dump, and you detect it through kubectl describe showing reason OOMKilled and exit code one hundred thirty-seven.

Step 5: The logs steer the engineer to the right fix: a Java heap OutOfMemoryError means grow the heap or fix a heap leak and analyze the dump, while an OOMKilled with a healthy heap means investigate native memory with Native Memory Tracking and leave more headroom below the container limit.

```text
[INFO] [startup] HEAP=2MB, NON-HEAP=7MB (Metaspace+CodeCache). Container counts BOTH + direct + stacks.
[INFO] Flags that preserve evidence in Kubernetes:
[INFO]   -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
[INFO]   -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps   (MOUNTED PVC, not /tmp)
[INFO]   terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120 (dump finishes writing)
[INFO]   -Xmx / MaxRAMPercentage BELOW the container limit (headroom)
[INFO] Distinguish failures:
[INFO]   Java heap OOM  → logs show 'OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space' + dump written
[INFO]   K8s OOMKilled  → kubectl describe pod: Reason=OOMKilled, exit 137; often NO dump
[SEVERE] Java heap OOM caught: Java heap space (heap dump written to -XX:HeapDumpPath)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Pod (container limit = 1Gi cgroup)
    │ total memory = HEAP + Metaspace + stacks + CodeCache + direct + overhead
    │
    ├─ Java HEAP fills (bounded by -Xmx)
    │     │ JVM throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
    │     ▼
    │   -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
    │     write dump → -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps (MOUNTED PVC)
    │     grace period 120s → dump finishes → SURVIVES restart
    │
    └─ TOTAL memory > 1Gi (heap maybe fine!)
          │ kernel OOM killer terminates process (OOMKilled, exit 137)
          ▼
        kubectl describe pod → Reason: OOMKilled
        often NO dump (JVM never ran its handler)
        → investigate NATIVE memory: jcmd VM.native_memory

  Pitfall: -Xmx == container limit → no headroom → OOMKilled with healthy heap
  Fix: MaxRAMPercentage ~60% so non-heap fits under the cap
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — OOMKilled vs Java Heap OutOfMemoryError ═══

  Aspect        Java heap OOM              K8s OOMKilled
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Who throws    JVM (Java exception)       Linux kernel (SIGKILL)
  Scope         Java heap only (-Xmx)      whole container (cgroup)
  Counts        heap objects               heap+Metaspace+stacks+

  Evidence      stack trace + heap dump    kubectl: Reason=OOMKilled,
                                           exit 137; often NO dump
  Detect        app logs, .hprof           kubectl describe/top pod
  Fix           raise -Xmx / fix heap leak native mem (NMT), lower -Xmx,
                                           add headroom (MaxRAMPercentage)

  Capture-in-K8s checklist:
 -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
 -XX:HeapDumpPath = MOUNTED volume (NOT /tmp, not ephemeral)
 terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ time to write full dump
 volume sized ≥ heap size
 -Xmx / MaxRAMPercentage below container limit (headroom)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Capturing a heap dump in Kubernetes has a trap that a lot of people learn the hard way, because containers are ephemeral. I enable dash XX plus HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so the JVM writes a dump automatically when it throws an OutOfMemoryError, but the critical detail is where it writes. If I point HeapDumpPath at something like slash tmp, the container's filesystem is wiped on restart, and since an OutOfMemoryError usually causes a restart, the very dump I need vanishes with the evidence. So I point HeapDumpPath at a path backed by a mounted persistent volume, a PersistentVolumeClaim, so the dump survives the pod's death and I can retrieve it afterward. Writing a dump of a multi-gigabyte heap also takes many seconds, and Kubernetes only waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, thirty by default, before forcibly killing the pod, so I raise that grace period enough for the full dump to finish writing, and I size the volume to hold a dump about the size of the heap.

The second half of this question is the diagnostic distinction, and it is one I have had to make in real incidents. A Java OutOfMemoryError for Java heap space is thrown by the JVM itself when the Java heap, bounded by dash Xmx, cannot satisfy an allocation. It is a Java-level exception, it triggers the heap-dump-on-OOM behavior, and the total container memory may have been perfectly healthy. A Kubernetes OOMKilled is a completely different thing: it is the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminating the process because the container exceeded its cgroup memory limit, and that limit counts everything, the heap plus Metaspace plus thread stacks plus the Code Cache plus direct and native memory plus JVM overhead. An OOMKilled is not a Java exception at all; the process is killed abruptly, so usually no heap dump gets written because the JVM never ran its handler.

I tell them apart by where I look. For an OOMKilled, kubectl describe pod shows the container's last state with reason OOMKilled and an exit code of one hundred thirty-seven, and kubectl top pod shows memory pinned at the limit. For a Java heap OutOfMemoryError, the application logs contain the OutOfMemoryError Java heap space stack trace and the heap dump is produced on the mounted volume.

The senior insight I always close with is that the two failures point to different fixes. A Java heap OutOfMemoryError means the heap is too small or there is a heap leak, so I grow dash Xmx or fix the leak and analyze the dump in MAT. An OOMKilled while the heap graphs look healthy means native memory is the culprit, such as direct buffers, thread stacks, or Metaspace, so I investigate with Native Memory Tracking using jcmd VM native memory summary rather than a heap dump. The classic banking incident is a service whose dash Xmx was set equal to the container limit, leaving no headroom for non-heap memory, so it was OOMKilled while the heap looked fine, and the fix was to set the heap well below the container limit, these days using the container-aware MaxRAMPercentage flag so the JVM automatically reserves room for everything else.

---

keyPoints: Distinguish OOMKilled (K8s memory limit) from Java OOM (heap limit)
OOMKilled: container exceeded memory limit — increase resources.limits.memory
Java OOM: heap exhausted — increase -Xmx or fix the leak
